title: Unlocking superplasticity in medium and high-entropy alloys
abstract: Abstract Superplasticity, the capacity of materials to sustain extraordinary tensile elongations at elevated temperatures, underpins a range of advanced metal-forming technologies. Conventionally, it is achieved in fine-grained alloys where deformation is dominated by grain-boundary sliding, accommodated by diffusion and dislocation activity. The advent of medium- and high-entropy alloys (M/HEAs), with their high chemical complexity and unconventional phase stability, offers new pathways to superplastic behavior beyond traditional alloy systems. Although investigated only recently, several M/HEAs already exhibit elongations that rival or exceed those of classical superplastic materials, particularly when ultrafine or metastable microstructures are engineered. Here, we review progress in understanding superplastic deformation in M/HEAs, emphasizing the interplay among composition, initial microstructure, thermomechanical processing, and microstructural evolution during high-temperature deformation. We discuss approaches to generating the fine-grained structures necessary for grain-boundary sliding, including severe plastic deformation and tailored heat treatments. We further highlight dynamic phenomena such as phase transformations, evolving grain-boundary chemistry, and deformation-induced grain refinement that can enhance plasticity in these systems. These mechanisms often shift the balance of deformation processes, enabling large elongations even outside classical criteria. Finally, we outline key challenges for application, including cost, scalability, recyclability, and microstructural stability.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: For decades, the formability of metallic alloys has been fundamental to engineering progress, serving as the basis for manufacturing intricate shapes in critical technologies such as engines, aircraft, rockets, and automobiles. The enabling phenomenon is superplasticity 1 , in which materials exhibit extraordinary tensile elongations, often greater than 400% and, in extreme cases, surpassing 1000%, without necking or failure 2 . Such elongations are only accessible at elevated temperatures, where strength is reduced, but deformation mechanisms such as grain-boundary sliding (GBS) dominate. The exploitation of superplasticity permits near-net-shape forming, minimizes secondary processing, and opens pathways for producing geometries that conventional methods cannot achieve. Historically, superplasticity has been observed primarily in fine-grained aluminum (Al), magnesium (Mg), and titanium (Ti) alloys, in which refined microstructures promote extensive GBS.

The mid-2000s saw the emergence of an unconventional alloy design concept that employed multi-principal-element alloys with near-equiatomic compositions in the 5–35 at.% range to form simple solid solutions 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 . These alloys, defined by their configurational entropy as medium- and high-entropy alloys (M/HEAs), were developed with the intent of leveraging high entropy to counteract mixing enthalpy, thus stabilizing simple solid-solution phases (face-centered cubic (fcc), body-centered cubic (bcc), or hexagonal close-packed (hcp)) instead of complex intermetallics or amorphous phases 7 . The resulting compositional complexity imparts distinctive mechanical and functional characteristics, making MEAs and HEAs promising candidates for advanced engineering applications 8 ,  9 – 10 .

Research into superplasticity in M/HEAs is still relatively young compared to conventional Al, Ti, or Mg alloys. Nevertheless, several studies have demonstrated that these multicomponent alloys can achieve elongations indicative of superplastic behavior, provided that the microstructural and testing conditions are optimized. For widespread adoption, these alloys must also demonstrate strong formability, enabling the production of intricate parts and components. The inherent stability of fine microstructures in M/HEAs at high temperatures makes them particularly suitable for superplastic forming applications. The potential of M/HEAs for superplastic forming is not merely a function of the inherent or universal stability of fine microstructures. Rather, it is highly driven by composition- and processing-dependent mechanisms retarding grain growth at elevated temperatures. These mechanisms include solute drag, sluggish or heterogeneous diffusion in the selected alloy systems, grain-boundary segregation, and, inevitably, the precipitation- or phase-boundary-assisted pinning. Furthermore, superplasticity should not be assumed for all M/HEAs, but under critical conditions where a fine and mostly equiaxed microstructure with a high fraction of mobile high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) is retained during deformation and when grain-boundary sliding (GBS) is effectively accommodated without excessive cavitation. Furthermore, microstructural stability should be used cautiously in the physical metallurgy of M/HEAs, as it does not necessarily refer to resistance to thermal evolution. It is rather the ability of a given alloy, under specific/controlled processing and testing conditions, to retain microstructural features (grain size, texture) and phase morphology compatible with sustained GBS. Despite this progress, only a limited number of review articles have specifically addressed superplasticity in M/HEAs; meanwhile, existing reviews discuss general microstructural characteristics and mechanical behavior rather than superplastic deformation 11 , 12 .

Therefore, this review aims to summarize recent advances in the emerging field of superplasticity in M/HEAs, with a focus on the initial microstructures, phase stability, and governing deformation mechanisms. In addition to summarizing current research, we identify key barriers and outline opportunities to promote future progress in both fundamental understanding and industrial applications of superplastic M/HEAs.

sections.heading: Fundamentals of superplasticity
paragraphs: The concept of superplasticity has its roots in early metallurgical research on eutectic alloys. In 1934, Lead-tin (Pb-Sn) and Bismuth-Tin (Bi-Sn) systems displayed extraordinary elongations of nearly 2000% following extrusion and extended aging 13 . Interest in the phenomenon resurfaced in the early 1960s, particularly after the influential 1962 review paper 14 , which highlighted studies on the ductility of eutectic and eutectoid alloys across temperature ranges. These works underscored the importance of order-disorder and metastable transformations, which enhance atomic and vacancy mobility and facilitate GBS. The interplay between dislocations and vacancies near transformation temperatures was recognized as the principal driver of superplastic deformation. By 1982, these principles were formalized through the sigmoidal stress–strain rate relationship identified in Zn-22Al alloys 15 , forming the basis for modern superplasticity models 16 ,  17 – 18 . In essence, superplasticity is defined by unusually high elongations ( > 400%), low flow stresses, and a strong strain-rate sensitivity coefficient ( m ) of approximately 0.3 – 0.5 1 , 19 , collectively distinguishing it from typical high-temperature creep processes.

For GBS to dominate, an appropriate combination of microstructural characteristics and testing conditions must be satisfied 17 , 23 : (1) fine grain size (d ≤ 10 µm, preferably <1 µm) to enhance sliding. (2) elevated temperatures (≥0.5 T m ) to promote boundary mobility, and (3) intermediate strain rates (10 −4 –10 −2  s −1 ) where GBS is maximized and competing mechanisms are suppressed. Because superplasticity primarily occurs at elevated temperatures, a strong resistance to grain growth is necessary to allow the dislocation and diffusion components to act in synergy to attain the high elongations 15 . If diffusion is too slow (due to sluggish kinetics), cavitation may dominate; if dislocations dominate, elongation drops, and necking occurs. Resistance to grain growth is often related to the existence of secondary phases that limit grain-boundary migration; thus, while superplasticity is possible in single-phase alloys, most superplastic alloys are multi-phase materials 19 . This is via the Zener pinning effect, which exerts a drag force that counteracts the thermodynamic driving pressure for boundary migration. The role of secondary phases in superplasticity is governed by their size, volume fraction, morphology, distribution, and mechanical compatibility with the surrounding matrix. From a Zener-pinning perspective, grain-boundary pinning scales approximately with  f/r , where  f  is the particle volume fraction, and  r  is the particle radius. Fine, uniformly distributed particles therefore provide effective resistance to grain growth, whereas coarse particles contribute little to boundary stabilization. Conversely, excessive fractions of hard or brittle secondary phases, particularly σ and μ phases, increase strain incompatibility and interfacial stresses, promoting cavity nucleation and premature failure. Superplastic performance therefore depends on balancing the benefits of grain-boundary pinning against the detrimental effects of damage accumulation during grain-boundary sliding. Hence, among the microstructural processes that control grain stability and enable the formation of fine-grained structures during deformation, dynamic recrystallization (DRX) stands out as a key phenomenon.

Recrystallization represents one of the most fundamental processes governing the microstructure of metals, involving the nucleation and growth of new grains. It is broadly categorized into static recrystallization (SRX) and DRX 24 . SRX occurs during post-deformation annealing, typically above ~0.5 T m , while DRX takes place during straining 25 , 26 . Both cases involve the gradual transformation from sub-grains with low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) to high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). However, SRX does not necessarily produce a uniform equiaxed microstructure 24 . Its effectiveness depends on the stored deformation energy, boundary mobility, solute drag, and the pinning pressure exerted by second-phase particles. For alloys containing stable or densely distributed particles, grain-boundary migration may be sufficiently restricted that SRX remains incomplete or spatially heterogeneous 24 . During superplastic deformation, by contrast, the additional driving force generated by plastic straining, grain-boundary sliding incompatibilities, and dislocation accumulation can promote DRX 24 , enabling the progressive formation of finer equiaxed grains under loading.

Superplasticity at high temperatures is closely associated with DRX, since straining during hot deformation naturally triggers this recrystallization pathway. The resulting DRX grain size is influenced by deformation conditions such as temperature, strain, and diffusion rates. DRX in superplasticity is a double-edged sword: while it can continuously refine grains to facilitate GBS, it may also induce grain growth that suppresses sliding and, eventually, ductility. Thus, achieving a balance between continuous refinement and microstructural stability is critical to attaining an excellent superplastic response.

The presumed sluggish diffusion in M/HEAs, combined with their high chemical complexity and associated thermal stability, has led to the expectation of remarkable superplastic properties 27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 – 31 . However, recent findings challenge this assumption, revealing instances of phase decomposition and polymorphic transitions 32 ,  33 ,  34 – 35 . Importantly, it has become clear that the nature of the constituent elements plays a more decisive role in diffusion behavior than the overall number of components 36 . Also, grain-growth kinetics of single-phase M/HEAs have been shown to align closely with those of traditional alloys 37 . As such, their superplastic properties may not be uniquely determined by the proposed core effects (i.e., high-entropy, sluggish diffusion, severe lattice distortion, short-range order, and cocktail effects) but instead follow the same limitations as conventional alloys 5 , 6 .

As with conventional alloy systems, secondary phase formation in M/HEAs proceeds either by spinodal decomposition or nucleation and growth, governed by thermodynamic stability and diffusion kinetics. Spinodal decomposition is favored when atomic pairs exhibit near-zero or mildly positive mixing enthalpies, producing local compositional modulations in an unstable solid solution. Conversely, more negative mixing enthalpies promote precipitation through the formation of energetically stable, ordered or disordered intermetallic compounds 38 ,  39 – 40 . As such, both processes are expected to influence superplasticity by stabilizing grain boundaries, i.e., spinodal decomposition through gradual chemical modulation and precipitation through discrete particle pinning. Hence, whether in single-phase or multiphase M/HEA systems, a balance between these mechanisms is essential for achieving sustained GBS and enhanced superplastic elongations.

sections.heading: Classical models for superplasticity and limitations for advanced material systems
paragraphs: Several classical models have been developed to describe the microscopic mechanisms that accommodate superplastic flow, broadly categorized into diffusional and dislocation-based frameworks. The Ashby-Verrall model 41  attributes accommodation to atomic diffusion around triple junctions, where atoms migrate from compressed to tensile regions (Fig.  1a ). This mechanism parallels the Nabarro-Herring 42 , 43  and Coble creep 44  models, all of which successfully explain grain switching and stability. However, they lack correlation between mass transport and local stress distribution, prompting refinements such as the Lee-Spingarn-Nix model 45 , 46 , which introduced directed diffusion and spheroidization during grain switching to reduce interfacial energy (Fig.  1b ). Despite its conceptual appeal, in-situ evidence for spheroidization remains elusive, emphasizing the need for modern high-resolution microscopy approaches to assess diffusion-controlled accommodation. Fig. 1 Classical models for understanding microscopic deformation accommodation during superplasticity. a  Ashby-Verrall model; Reproduced with permission from ref.  41 , copyright (Elsevier, 1973).  b  Lee-Spingarn-Nix model; Reproduced with permission from ref.  46 , copyright (Elsevier, 1978).  c  Ball-Hutchison model,  d  Gifkins’ Core-mantle model; Reproduced with permission from ref.  47 , copyright (Elsevier, 1997).  e  Langdon’s theory; Reproduced with permission from ref.  17 , copyright (Elsevier, 1994).

In contrast, dislocation-based models describe GBS accommodated by dislocation motion. The Ball-Hutchison model 47 , 48  proposes that cooperative GBS generates stress concentrations at grain junctions, which are relaxed through dislocation activity in neighboring grains (Fig.  1c ). Yet, the absence of direct evidence for these dislocation processes, often inferred only from post-mortem transmission electron microscopy (TEM), limits its predictive accuracy. The Gifkins’ core-mantle model 49  suggests that dislocation activity is confined to the mantle region near boundaries, leaving the grain core largely dislocation-free (Fig.  1d ). Although supported by microstructural observations, the model lacks real-time validation, and recent findings of variable mantle thickness call for in-situ investigations for deeper mechanistic insight.

sections.heading: Superplasticity in single-phase fcc M/HEAs
paragraphs: The most widely studied HEA for superplasticity is the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, also known as the Cantor alloy. This fcc-structured HEA demonstrates remarkable ductility, thermal stability, and cryogenic fracture toughness, making it a model system for investigating high-temperature deformation 54 . Its strength decreases steadily from cryogenic to elevated temperatures (15–1273 K), accessing multiple deformation mechanisms including dislocation slip, twinning, and phase transformation 55 ,  56 ,  57 ,  58 – 59 . Superplasticity in this single-phase alloy was first reported by Reddy et al. 60 , who observed elongations up to ~320% at 1023 K and 10 −4  s −1  (Fig.  2a ). Numerous cavity stringers along the tensile direction were observed in the ~320% elongation sample (Fig.  2b ), which limited the ductility and likely reduced the efficiency of GBS. As the strain rate increased, the strain-rate sensitivity coefficient ( m ) dropped from 0.59 to 0.25, suggesting a shift from superplastic to non-superplastic behavior 2 . The microstructure of the sample before the tensile testing possessed a recrystallized microstructure with an average grain size of 1.4 µm (Fig.  2c ), which decreased in the 10 − 1  s −1  deformed sample (Fig.  2d ) and increased in the 10 −4  s −1  deformed sample (Fig.  2e ). While DRX produced ~1 µm grains at high strain rates, limited elongations were observed due to discontinuous boundary formation. Meanwhile, grain coarsening at low strain rates reduced GBS activity, resulting in profuse cavitation. This demonstrates that stable ultrafine grains are also essential for sustained GBS in HEAs, just as in conventional alloys 2 , 21 , 61 . Fig. 2 Superplasticity in the equiatomic Cantor alloy. a  Tensile stress-strain curves of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples;  b  scanning electron microscopy (SEM) surface morphology image of 1023 K 10 −4  s −1  tensile-fractured sample;  c – e  Microstructures of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples. Reproduced with permission from ref.  60 , copyright (Taylor & Francis, 2017).

To achieve superplasticity, the alloy’s processing history is critical. Conventional thermomechanical treatments, such as rolling followed by recrystallization annealing, typically refine microstructures only to the micrometer scale or, at best, a few hundred nanometers when annealed at intermediate temperatures. In contrast, severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques such as high-pressure torsion (HPT), equal-channel angular pressing (ECAP), and friction stir processing (FSP) offer far greater refinement capability required for GBS during superplastic deformation 62 ,  63 ,  64 – 65 . HPT-processed Cantor alloys exhibit extreme grain refinement (~10 nm) (see Fig.  3a ) and high strength (1.4 GPa yield), but have poor ductility (~4%) 66 . Because HPT generates severe internal stresses, HPT-processed samples must be annealed to relieve these stresses and restore an optimal strength-ductility balance. Controlled annealing or microalloying introduces secondary phases that stabilize the microstructure and enhance GBS 67 ,  68 – 69 . For example, Ti addition (CrMnFeCoNiTi 0.1 ) generated ~12 vol.% Cr-rich bcc and σ precipitates during high-temperature deformation, maintaining ~400 nm grains and attaining elongations of up to ~830% at 973 K and 10 −2  s −1  as shown in Fig.  3b, c 68 . Similarly, Al additions to the Cantor alloy produced Ni-Al-rich B2 and Cr-rich σ phases during deformation, resulting in a triplex fcc-B2-σ structure and elongations exceeding 1100% 69 . These precipitates inhibit grain growth, ensuring GBS dominates during deformation. Non-equiatomic HEAs, such as V 10 Cr 15 Mn 5 Fe 35 Co 10 Ni 25 , subjected to HPT, developed an average grain size of 30 nm (Fig.  3d ) and achieved an impressive superplastic elongation of ~700% at 1073 K and 3.3 × 10 −3  s −1 , as shown in Fig.  3e . The electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) inverse pole figure (IPF) maps (Fig.  3f ) of the sample at the grip and gauge regions showed an equiaxed microstructure formed at this temperature and strain rate, which indicates superplasticity, proceeded mainly by GBS. However, grain growth occurred in all regions irrespective of the formation of the σ precipitates due to the high temperature. This trend indicates that the sufficient enhancement of grain recovery at elevated temperatures likely nullifies the grain growth retardation effect of secondary precipitates 70 , 71 . Fig. 3 Superplasticity in the HPT-processed Cantor alloy variants. a  TEM image with a corresponding selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern of the HPT-processed CrMnFeCoNi sample. Reproduced with permission from refs.  67 , copyright (Elsevier, 2017);  b  Macroscopic images of the HPT-processed CrMnFeCoNiTi 0.1  samples before and after tensile testing;  c  SEM micrograph of the 973 K 10 −2  s −1  tensile-deformed CrMnFeCoNiTi 0.1  HEA sample. Reproduced with permission from refs.  68 . copyright (Elsevier, 2018);  d  TEM image and corresponding SAED pattern of the V 10 Cr 15 Mn 5 Fe 35 Co 10 Ni 25  HEA subjected to HPT;  e  Effect of strain rate on the tensile stress-strain response at 1073 K;  f  EBSD-IPF maps of the V 10 Cr 15 Mn 5 Fe 35 Co 10 Ni 25  sample after tensile deformation at 1073 K and 3.3 × 10 −3  s −1 . Adapted with permission from refs.  71 , copyright (Elsevier, 2019).

Medium-entropy derivatives such as the Al-modified CrCoNi exhibited even higher elongations (~1175%) through GBS stabilized by the dynamic precipitation of the B2 and σ phases, while in some cases, accompanied by localized intergranular melting that promotes boundary accommodation 72 . The formation of a thin Al-rich liquid film along grain boundaries was attributed to deformation-induced Al segregation and the formation of supersaturated vacancy-solute complexes during dynamic precipitation.

Across these studies, single-phase M/HEAs are shown to be only “quasi-stable”, with thermal decomposition reactions forming secondary phases such as σ and bcc at elevated temperatures 66 . While such phase formation can adversely affect properties such as oxidation or corrosion resistance, it is beneficial for superplasticity by suppressing grain growth and helping maintain equiaxed microstructures during GBS. This implies that the supposedly “slow” diffusion and grain-growth kinetics in M/HEAs are composition-specific rather than inherent.

A common feature among fcc-structured superplastic M/HEAs is a relatively low strain-rate sensitivity ( m  ≈ 0.3) 67 , 68 , 71 , below the ideal  m  = 0.5 typical for conventional superplastic flow 2 , 21 . In conventional alloys,  m  ≈ 0.3 corresponds to solute-drag or viscous glide creep, limiting elongations to ~200–300% 21 , 73 . Yet, M/HEAs can achieve elongations well above 400%, indicating that solute-drag creep is not operative and that GBS dominates even with low  m . The reduced  m  has been tentatively linked to grain growth during deformation, though this remains speculative; this underscores the need for further investigations into atomic-level chemical complexity and grain-boundary diffusion kinetics in M/HEAs. These findings reveal that optimized superplasticity in single-phase M/HEAs does not stem directly from their intrinsic “core effects” but from a synergistic combination of grain refinement, precipitate-assisted microstructural stabilization, and diffusion- or dislocation-mediated GBS. Hence, microalloying single-phase fcc M/HEAs with elements such as Ti and Al introduces stronger negative mixing enthalpies, promoting microstructural instability at elevated temperatures and driving the dynamic precipitation of secondary phases 27 . These phases effectively pin grain boundaries, which enhances microstructural stability and sustains GBS-dominated deformation. Consequently, the balance between grain refinement, boundary stability, and GBS emerges as the central mechanism governing superplasticity in single-phase M/HEAs.

sections.heading: Superplasticity in refractory M/HEAs
paragraphs: Superplasticity in refractory M/HEAs should be viewed as a microstructure-enabled high-temperature deformation phenomenon rather than an intrinsic characteristic of bcc refractory alloys. In contrast to fcc Cantor-type M/HEAs, refractory systems generally require substantially higher absolute temperatures to achieve comparable homologous temperatures because of their exceptionally high melting points 51 , 74 ,  75 ,  76 – 77 . Under these conditions, deformation is governed by the interplay between screw- and edge-dislocation mobility, dynamic recovery, dynamic recrystallization (DRX), precipitation stability, and oxidation resistance, all of which strongly influence the evolution of the microstructure during deformation 78 , 79 . Consequently, the mechanisms governing superplasticity in refractory M/HEAs differ fundamentally from those established for fine-grained fcc alloys and should not be interpreted using the classical framework in which grain-boundary sliding (GBS) operates within a uniformly ultrafine-grained microstructure 76 , 80 , 81 .

Instead, recent studies suggest that superplasticity in refractory M/HEAs emerges through deformation-induced microstructural evolution. In HfNbTaTiZr, high-temperature deformation, localized grain-boundary bulging, and DRX progressively generate fine-grained necklace structures surrounding coarse, unrecrystallized grains 79 . These dynamically recrystallized regions provide the high-angle grain boundaries required for GBS, while the coarse bcc matrix continues to accommodate strain through dislocation slip and high-temperature creep 11 , 78 , 79 . Rather than competing, these mechanisms operate cooperatively, producing a heterogeneous, dual-scale microstructure in which GBS, dislocation plasticity, and creep collectively sustain large tensile elongations. This behavior challenges the conventional paradigm that superplasticity requires a uniformly fine-grained starting microstructure and instead demonstrates that deformation itself can generate the microstructural conditions necessary for superplastic flow.

The emergence of lightweight refractory M/HEAs further extends this concept toward practical forming applications. In Ti-V-Zr-Nb-Mo-based refractory MEAs 82 , coarse-grained superplasticity has been linked to the sequential activation of dislocation slip, DRX, and GBS, enabling large elongations while preserving high post-forming strength 82 . These observations suggest that future alloy design should shift from maximizing grain refinement alone toward engineering controlled microstructural heterogeneity. Stabilizing DRX regions through nanoprecipitate pinning, promoting controlled DRX-band formation, tailoring phase stability, and expanding oxidation-resistant processing windows may provide more effective routes to superplasticity than simply producing ultrafine-grained microstructures. In this framework, refractory M/HEAs represent an alternative superplasticity paradigm in which deformation-induced microstructural evolution, rather than the initial grain structure, governs the onset and stability of superplastic flow.

sections.heading: Superplasticity in multiphase HEAs
paragraphs: Single-phase fcc M/HEAs generally exhibit low yield strength at room temperature, while bcc-structured counterparts suffer from poor ductility 9 . To overcome these inherent limitations, multiphase alloys incorporating both ductile and hard phases have been developed to balance strength and ductility 83 . However, phase interfaces can introduce strain incompatibility and stress concentrations that promote embrittlement. In conventional alloys, multiphase microstructures are known to enhance superplasticity by stabilizing fine grains at elevated temperatures 2 , 21 . Similarly, in M/HEAs, secondary and tertiary phases can inhibit grain coarsening while allowing limited dislocation motion, conditions necessary for GBS-controlled superplastic flow.

Al-alloying is the most common go-to method for forming multiphase microstructures in M/HEAs due to its strong bcc-forming tendency, leading to ordered B2 or L2 1  precipitates, which are significantly harder than the fcc matrix 84 . The equiatomic AlCuCrFeNiCo alloy was the first HEA reported to exhibit superplasticity 85 ,  86 ,  87 – 88 . After multiaxial forging, a refined four-phase structure (fcc, B2, σ, and Co-Cr-Fe-type fcc) developed, with evidence of both spinodal decomposition and precipitation. The four distinct phases labeled 1 to 4 in the SEM-BSE image of Fig.  4a  correspond to the Cu-rich fcc, Ni-Al-rich B2, σ, and Co-Cr-Fe-type fcc phases, respectively. Figure  4b  presents the TEM image of the four phases, and the SAED patterns in Fig.  4c  confirmed the respective phases. Superplastic elongations were reached at 1173 K and 1273 K, even though an impressive ductility of ~330% was observed at 1073 K and a strain rate of 10 −2  s −1 , as shown in Fig.  4d-f . The general overview of the samples tested at 1273 K is depicted in the photograph of Fig.  4g , which clearly demonstrates that the 1273 K 10 −2  s −1  sample displays the highest elongation with almost no observable necking. The maximum elongation of 1240% at 1273 K and 10 −2  s −1  ( m  ≈ 0.5) was attributed to GBS assisted by dislocation glide and partial phase dissolution. Figure  4h  shows that the deformed microstructure was similar to the initial microstructure, as no notable grain growth occurred. The inherent microstructural stability suppressed grain growth, promoting steady-state flow and confirming the effectiveness of multiphase stabilization. Fig. 4 Microstructure and tensile properties of an MF equiatomic AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA. a  SEM-BSE micrograph;  b  TEM image depicting four phases;  c  SAED patterns corresponding to different phases.  d – f  Tensile stress-strain curves at different temperatures.  g  Photographs of tensile samples before and after deformation at 1273 K.  h  SEM-BSE image of the 1273 K tensile deformed sample at 10 −2  s −1 . Reproduced with permission from refs.  86 , copyright (Springer Nature, 2013).

Subsequent investigations further established that the coexistence of ductile (fcc) and ordered (B2 or σ) phases enhances GBS by stabilizing grain size and facilitating diffusion-assisted sliding. For example, the friction-stir-processed CoCrFeNiCu HEAs exhibited 620% elongation at 1223 K due to Cu-enabled phase separation, which promoted sliding and structural stability 89 . The addition of Al led to B2 precipitation (a harder phase than the Cu-rich fcc phase), which doubled the elongation (~1280%) via grain-growth suppression accelerated by the effectiveness of the harder B2 phase in pinning grain boundaries 90 . The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi 2.1  HEA achieved ~960% elongation at 1173 K, with B2 precipitation maintaining ultrafine equiaxed grains during deformation, even with numerous cavities during the tensile deformation 91 . Similarly, the B2 precipitates in the Al 5 Cr 20 Fe 35 Co 35 Ni 5  HEA processed by high-ratio differential speed rolling (HRDSR), stabilized the equiaxed matrix grains to achieve ~465 % at 973 K and 5 × 10 −4  s −1 92 . The Al-containing fcc/B2 HEAs show how superplasticity can be engineered through deformation-responsive phase stability 92 . In these alloys, B2 precipitation can refine grains, retard coarsening, and modify the accommodation of GBS. Recent work on the Al 0.5 CoCrFeNiCu HEA shows that deformation-induced B2 precipitation plays a stage-dependent role during superplastic flow 90 , 93 . This improves microstructural stability when fine and discontinuous, but can introduce interphase incompatibility when excessive. Similar trends in ultrafine-grained Al 5 Cr 20 Fe 35 Co 35 Ni 5  indicate that B2-assisted stabilization is most effective when precipitation, boundary mobility, and deformation-induced recovery evolve cooperatively during straining.

In HPT-processed duplex fcc/B2 Al 9 (CrMnFeCoNi) 91  HEA ultrafine structures (~1 µm fcc + ~500 nm B2) yielded extreme elongations (~2000%) and high strain-rate sensitivity ( m  = 0.47) 94 , nearly doubling that of single-phase counterparts 69 . The B2 phase provided both grain-growth inhibition and dislocation accommodation, while the limited σ fraction enhanced thermal stability. Compared to the single-phase Cantor and Al 9 (CrMnFeCoNi) 91  HEAs, where limited precipitate formation only partially stabilized nanograins, the pre-existing duplex structure of the fcc-B2 alloy provided inherent thermal stability and dislocation accommodation, enabling far greater elongations 69 , 94 . Al additions (≤9 at.%) to CrCoNi MEAs form duplex (fcc-B2) and triplex (fcc-B2-σ) microstructures depending on the thermomechanical processing and SPD route (Fig.  5a, b ). The duplex and triplex alloys are denoted as DP-MEA and TP-MEA for simplicity. The SEM-BSE images and corresponding energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) elemental maps revealed that the comprising elements were uniformly distributed in the fcc matrix, B2 precipitates as Ni-Al-rich, and the σ phase as Cr-rich (Fig.  5c, d ). Figures  5 e, f show the strain rate-dependent tensile tests at 1073 K, where the DP-MEA and TP-MEA displayed maximum elongations of ~1900% and ~1735% at strain rates of 5 × 10 −3  s −1  and 10 −2  s −1 , respectively. Figure  5g, h  show that both alloys formed an equiaxed fcc-B2-σ triplex microstructure after tensile deformation, which suggested that GBS assisted by intragranular dislocation motion within the equiaxed microstructure was the main deformation mechanism 95 , 96 . However, the variations in the phase fractions and grain sizes, especially the inability of the sigma phase to accommodate dislocations during GBS 97 . The higher σ-phase content (12%) and coarser grains of the TP-MEA promote stress localization and cavitation, reducing ductility. Although σ also refines and stabilizes the microstructure, its optimized control is vital for superior superplasticity 96 , 98 . Fig. 5 Influence of different starting microstructures on the superplastic elongations in the AlCoCrNi MEA. a ,  b  Sample preparation routes;  c ,  d  SEM-BSE images and EDS elemental maps;  e ,  f  Strain rate-dependent tensile stress-strain curves at 1073 K;  g ,  h  Deformation microstructural phase and EDS elemental maps of the DP- and TP-MEAs. Adapted with permission from ref.  96 , copyright (Elsevier, 2022).

Topologically close-packed (TCP) phases such as σ and µ, commonly observed in Cr- and Mo-containing HEAs 99 , 100 , significantly influence superplasticity. Their high hardness (~15 GPa) refines grains and resists coarsening, yet their complex crystal structure and high energy barrier make dislocation glide difficult, which leads to void formation and premature fracture 101 , 102 . Therefore, they can only be used in small quantities to boost strength at the expense of ductility, according to the tradeoff between strength and ductility 103 , or as pinning phases that help stabilize the microstructure during superplastic deformation 104 . TCP phases improve superplasticity within a narrow microstructural window. In Cr- and Mo-containing M/HEAs, σ and μ phases can retard grain growth due to the high hardness and limited mobility with strong boundary-pinning effects. However, the role of complex crystal structures and poor dislocation accommodation is characteristic of sites for interfacial stress concentration, cavity nucleation, and premature fracture. The balance can be expressed semi-quantitatively by comparing the pinning benefit, which scales approximately with  f/r , against the cavitation susceptibility, which increases with the density of hard matrix/TCP interfaces, where  f  is the TCP-phase volume fraction, and  r  is the characteristic particle radius. Fine, discontinuously distributed TCP particles can stabilize equiaxed grains at relatively low volume fractions, whereas coarse particles, high σ fractions, or interconnected TCP networks promote damage-controlled failure. Thus, the relevant design criterion is not TCP-phase fraction alone, but the combined effect of  f/r , interparticle spacing, phase morphology, and plastic compatibility with the surrounding fcc or B2 matrix.

Sohn et al. 105  reported that the single-phase fcc VCoNi MEA exhibited limited superplasticity, whereas a duplex κ/σ microstructure achieved elongations up to ~450% at 1073 K and 10 −2  s −1 , as shown in Fig.  6a . The VCoNi alloy maintains a stable fcc structure above 1173 K but undergoes a eutectoid reaction at 1073 K, forming κ and σ phases 106 . Figure  6b  revealed that the fine κ/σ duplex (~90% κ, ~10% σ) was conducive to optimal superplasticity due to the κ grain pinning by the σ phase; nevertheless, void nucleation around σ grains limited elongation (Fig.  6c ). Interestingly, increasing σ content during deformation (i.e., dynamic σ precipitation) enhanced stress concentration, reducing elongation to ~270% in (CoNiV) 93 Al 7 , which possessed an initial fcc-L2 1  microstructure 107 . Comparable effects were seen in the friction-stir-processed Fe 42 Mn 28 Co 10 Cr 15 Si 5,  which reached ~550% elongation at 973 K and 10 −3  s −1  (Fig.  6d ) through an fcc-hcp-σ triplex structure 108 . Although σ particles constrained grain growth, they promoted cavitation at fcc-σ interfaces, causing premature fracture (Fig.  6e, f ) 109 . Similarly, the µ phase, typical in Mo-rich HEAs, enhances grain refinement but also promotes void formation 110 ,  111 ,  112 – 113 . These findings underline the dual role of TCP phases in providing structural stability while concurrently limiting ductility through cavitation. Fig. 6 Superplasticity in M/HEAs with TCP phases. a  Tensile stress-strain curves at 1073 K;  b  EBSD-IQ image of tensile-deformed microstructure overlaid with phase maps;  c  ECCI micrograph showing void formation of the duplex VCoNi superplastic MEA. Reproduced with permission from ref.  105 , copyright (Elsevier, 2020).  d  Stress-strain curves of the Fe 42 Mn 28 Co 10 Cr 15 Si 5  HEA samples at 973 K;  e  EBSD-IQ image superimposed with phase color;  f  SEM images of the tensile deformed Fe 42 Mn 28 Co 10 Cr 15 Si 5  HEA samples. Adapted with permission from ref.  108 , copyright (Elsevier, 2020).

Superplasticity in multiphase M/HEAs emerges from the interplay of grain stabilization and cavitation control. Deformable fcc and B2 domains can support GBS through dislocation glide, boundary diffusion, and local stress relaxation, whereas hard σ and μ phases suppress grain growth but promote embrittlement when their fraction, size, or connectivity becomes excessive. Eutectic M/HEAs extend this design principle by introducing stable duplex or multiple-phase architectures in the starting microstructure, providing pre-existing phase boundaries that can sustain GBS at technologically relevant strain rates. However, these same interfaces can accelerate cavity nucleation when interphase plastic compatibility is poor. Therefore, the key design variables for multiphase and eutectic M/HEAs are phase fraction, interphase spacing, phase continuity, morphology, and compatibility.

sections.heading: High-strain rate superplasticity in HEAs
paragraphs: The strain rate is a very important parameter that determines the superplastic flow. In every alloy system, there is an optimum deformation period where GBS becomes very favorable to accommodate high superplastic elongations irrespective of cavitation or dynamic grain growth. Conventional superplasticity typically occurs at moderate to low strain rates (10 −4 –10 −3  s -1 ), which increases production times during mass-forming operations 21 , 114 . This trend creates unintended costs and even climate repercussions that are unfavorable for mass economic production. To offset this challenge, major efforts have been placed on shifting superplasticity to higher strain-rate regimes to reduce commercial production times 63 , 64 , 115 . For example, the commercial Al-Mg-Sc alloy recorded an impressive 2000% superplastic elongation at 723 K and a high-strain rate of 5.6 × 10 − 2  s −1 116 .

With the emergence of M/HEAs, achieving a high-strain-rate superplasticity (HSRS) in these alloys would exemplify a tremendous breakthrough for their commercial processing. HSRS is classified as a superplastic flow that occurs above 10 −2  s −1 . Especially since HSRS is difficult to obtain in high-strength alloys and would also offer substantial cost savings towards their commercialization. A summary of the elongations versus strain rate of M/HEAs at 973 K and 1073 K is shown in Fig.  7 . The plot presents the minimum elongation considered as superplasticity (i.e., the red-line demarcation). At 973 K, the Fe 42 Mn 28 Co 10 Cr 15 Si 5  HEA failed to show HSRS. Meanwhile, the V 10 Cr 15 Mn 5 Fe 35 Co 10 Ni 25  CrMnFeCoNi, and CrMnFeCoNiTi 0.1  HEAs all showed HSRS. The minor Ti addition to the Cantor alloy shifted the maximum superplastic elongation to the HSRS regime regardless of the smaller grain size of the Cantor alloy (10 nm), compared to the CrMnFeCoNiTi 0.1  (30 nm) 67 , 68 . The Al 9 (CrMnFeCoNi) 91  HEA samples demonstrated remarkable HSRS elongations, with up to an ~800% elongation at 973 K and 0.5 s −1 69 , 94 . Fig. 7 High-strain rate regimes in reported M/HEAs. The dependence of superplasticity on strain rates of reported HEAs at  a  973 K and  b  1073 K.

At 1073 K, the rapid grain coarsening of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA resulted in an overall diminished superplasticity (<400%) 67 . HSRS was absent in the Fe 55 Co 18 Cr 12.5 Ni 7 Mo 7.5  MEA 113 , while the V 10 Cr 15 Mn 5 Fe 35 Co 10 Ni 25  sample showed good superplasticity (~580%) at 10 −2  s −1 73 . The Al 9 (CrMnFeCoNi) 91  and Al 9 (CrCoNi) 91  samples displayed very impressive HSRS elongations, with an optimum elongation of ~2000% recorded at 0.05 s −1  for the Al 9 (CrMnFeCoNi) 91  HEA 69 , 72 , 94 , 96 . Nanocrystalline microstructures and powder metallurgy-processed conventional alloys were found to be more viable for displaying HSRS 117 . This characteristic indicates that grain refinement is key to shifting the optimum strain rate for superplasticity to the higher strain-rate levels. While the summary in Fig.  7  indicates that most M/HEAs are capable of attaining HSRS, no studies have been performed to determine the grain size threshold for attaining HSRS. Nevertheless, since all these M/HEAs were processed by SPD to achieve nanocrystalline structures, it is unclear to establish a correlation between the grain size and the optimal strain rate for peak superplasticity.

Generally, HSRS in M/HEAs is better understood as a dynamically stabilized fine-grain state rather than a simple consequence of SPD-induced nanocrystallinity. SPD provides the initial ultrafine or nanocrystalline structure, high HAGB fraction, stored defect density, and non-equilibrium boundaries needed to shift the optimum strain rate upward. However, high-rate elongation is sustained only when dynamic precipitation, DRX, solute segregation, or phase-boundary pinning prevents rapid coarsening and accommodates local strain incompatibilities. Recent studies have broadened the design philosophy for HSRS, and thus, there is no need to establish the optimum microstructure before testing, but it can be regenerated or stabilized during deformation 90 , 92 , 93 .

Another important factor is the phase distributions of these M/HEAs. So far, all the reported superplastic HEAs contain matrix phases of cubic structures and secondary phases that are present in the initial microstructure or form during high-temperature deformation. The hard TCP phases, such as the σ or µ phases that become available during the high-temperature deformation due to diffusion-based chemical partitioning effects, contribute to restricting rapid grain coarsening. This trend provides adequate surfaces for the grains to slide over each other for a prolonged period to achieve superplasticity. But these TCP phases simultaneously cause cavitation problems due to the inhomogeneous stress gradients that they create, especially at interfacial boundaries 105 . As such, the presence of secondary phases like the B2 phase in the starting microstructure is essential, since they offer an extra dislocation accommodation domain in addition to the fcc grains during GBS, so that when the σ phase appears, the formation of voids is delayed to achieve excellent superplastic elongations 94 . This is especially facilitated when dislocation accommodation is rapid because dislocations heal local incompatibilities quickly to prevent cavitation. Of course, the driving force for grain growth becomes intense at elevated temperatures and low-to-moderate strain rates. Hence, once significant grain growth occurs during deformation, the GBS mechanism gradually diminishes, and the deformation likely proceeds by diffusion or dislocation creep 2 , 21 .

Alternatively, deformation-induced or equilibrium segregation can produce thin, low-melting mobile interfacial layers that increase interfacial diffusivity, thereby simultaneously slowing matrix grain coarsening and dramatically enhancing accommodation by providing a fast viscous flow channel (liquid-assisted GBS) to attain HSRS 72 . Given that the factors that govern the transition from conventional superplasticity to HSRS in M/HEAs are not fully understood, comprehensive investigations are required to unravel the underlying mechanisms.

Ultimately, the opportunity lies not only in extending elongations but in controlling when, how, and at what strain rate superplasticity occurs. For single-phase microstructures, focusing on achieving ultrafine grains with dislocation-accommodated GBS is more plausible, whereas for multiphase microstructures, carefully managing precipitates to balance grain stabilization and cavitation risk is important.

sections.heading: Dislocation-mediated accommodation and decoupling of strain-rate sensitivity in superplastic M/HEAs
paragraphs: Classical theories of superplasticity establish a strong correlation between exceptionally high tensile elongation and a strain-rate sensitivity coefficient approaching  m  ≈ 0.5, which is consistent with GBS-dominated superplastic flow 1 , 2 , 15 , 17 , 21 , but the accommodation path, which could be lattice diffusion, grain-boundary diffusion, dislocation climb, or mixed diffusion-dislocation accommodation, is identifiable using activation-energy analysis, grain-size dependence, and microstructural factors. In conventional fine-grained alloys, deviations from this ideal condition typically signal a transition toward dislocation creep or solute-drag–controlled flow, accompanied by a rapid loss of ductility 17 , 21 , 73 . However, a growing body of experimental evidence in M/HEAs reveals a striking inconsistency with this classical paradigm: superplastic elongations exceeding 1000% are frequently achieved despite  m  values in the range of 0.3–0.4 67 ,  68 – 69 , 94 ,  95 – 96 .

The role of dislocation activity in superplastic M/HEAs should be interpreted with caution. In many fcc 3d-transition-element M/HEAs, the elements might generate large and severe lattice distortion, such as Al, Ti, or Mo, which are likely to promote secondary-phase formation. Consequently, the observed accommodation behavior cannot be attributed solely to lattice distortion in a single-phase solid solution. It may instead reflect the combined effects of GBS, dislocation activity within deformable fcc or B2 domains, solute drag, boundary segregation, and precipitation-assisted grain stabilization. A rigorous separation of these effects requires systematic comparison between genuinely single-phase alloys and alloys containing controlled fractions of B2, σ, μ, or other secondary phases.

This apparent decoupling between strain-rate sensitivity and attainable elongation suggests that the accommodation mechanisms operating during superplastic deformation in M/HEAs differ fundamentally from those in conventional alloys. Rather than being governed solely by diffusion-controlled processes, GBS in chemically complex alloys appears to be strongly assisted by dislocation-mediated accommodation mechanisms that are enhanced by compositional disorder, lattice distortion, and heterogeneous phase stability 17 , 48 ,  49 – 50 , 54 .

In M/HEAs, grain-boundary sliding generates pronounced local stress heterogeneities due to variations in boundary chemistry, misorientation, and interfacial strength 2 , 17 , 23 , 37 . These stress concentrations are not relaxed exclusively through atomic diffusion; instead, they promote intense, localized dislocation activity within adjacent grains or soft phases 48 , 49 , 61 , 65 . The presence of severe lattice distortion and strong solute–dislocation interactions in M/HEAs increases dislocation storage capacity and back-stress development, enabling effective stress redistribution without immediate strain localization or necking 50 ,  51 – 52 , 54 , 70 . Consequently, dislocations act not as the primary carriers of macroscopic plastic strain, but as efficient accommodation agents that stabilize GBS-dominated flow 17 , 48 , 49 , 54 .

This dislocation-assisted accommodation is particularly effective in multiphase or metastable M/HEAs, where deformable phases such as fcc or B2 domains coexist with harder phases that suppress grain growth 69 , 84 , 94 ,  95 – 96 . In such systems, dislocation motion within the softer phases can rapidly heal local incompatibilities at sliding grain boundaries, delaying cavitation even when hard TCP phases (e.g., σ or µ) are present 96 ,  97 – 98 , 104 , 105 . The result is a cooperative deformation mode in which GBS governs macroscopic strain accumulation, while dislocation activity governs local compatibility and stress relaxation 17 , 48 , 49 .

Importantly, this framework provides a mechanistic explanation for why high superplastic elongations can be sustained at m values significantly below the classical threshold of 0.5 67 ,  68 – 69 , 71 . In M/HEAs, the effectiveness of accommodation is no longer dictated solely by diffusion kinetics, but by the combined efficiency of dislocation-mediated stress redistribution, dynamic recrystallization, and deformation-induced phase evolution 24 , 61 , 67 , 71 . As a result, strain-rate sensitivity alone becomes an insufficient predictor of elongation in M/HEAs 21 , 67 , 94 . It remains a useful indicator of rate sensitivity and necking resistance, but it must be interpreted together with activation energy, grain-size evolution, phase stability, cavitation behavior, and evidence for the operative accommodation mechanism.

From a design perspective, this insight shifts the focus from maximizing m toward engineering microstructures that promote robust dislocation-assisted accommodation during GBS. Strategies such as controlled metastability, dynamic precipitation of deformable secondary phases, and heterogeneous grain structures can enhance accommodation capacity without relying exclusively on diffusion-dominated mechanisms 69 , 72 , 84 , 94 , 96 . In this sense, superplasticity in M/HEAs emerges not from the suppression of dislocation activity, but from its deliberate integration into a GBS-controlled deformation framework 17 , 48 , 49 , 54 .

Overall, the superplastic behavior of M/HEAs highlights a fundamental departure from classical superplasticity concepts. The ability of these alloys to sustain extreme elongations at moderate strain-rate sensitivities underscores the need for revised mechanistic models that explicitly incorporate dislocation-mediated accommodation in chemically complex, metastable microstructures 17 , 50 , 118 , 119 . Such models will be essential for developing predictive guidelines for next-generation superplastic alloys beyond the constraints of conventional design philosophies 118 , 119 .

sections.heading: Synthesis and comparative framework for dilute and M/HEAs
paragraphs: The comparison between conventional alloy systems and M/HEAs reveals a transformative conceptual shift in the research and design of superplastic materials. Historically, superplastic performance in metals has been anchored in the principle of microstructural stability. Fine grains are created through thermomechanical processing, and all subsequent design decisions, including processing temperatures, alloying additions, and strain rates, are imposed to preserve that refined microstructure and suppress grain growth, phase instability, or solute redistribution. The deformation process is treated as potentially destructive, and the goal is to maintain the microstructure in a “frozen” fine-grained state for as long as possible.

M/HEAs represent a departure from this preservation-based approach. Their intrinsic high configurational entropy, potentially sluggish diffusion, and complex phase interactions create a landscape of numerous design opportunities 120 . The new paradigm is controlled microstructural flexibility, i.e., the initial microstructure is purposely engineered to be responsive to stress, temperature, and strain rate. Deformation-induced phase transformations, DRX, dislocation or stacking fault accumulation, and interface migration are not suppressed; they are utilized to continually refine the microstructure, preserve equiaxed grains, and improve accommodation mechanisms. This enables a dynamically self-optimizing microstructure capable of sustaining superplastic flow that is theoretically beyond the limits of classical alloys.

This conceptual shift from preserving structure to manipulating its evolution carries significant implications for alloy design, thermodynamic tuning, kinetic control, and the mechanistic understanding of flow accommodation. The key distinctions in governing mechanisms, stability criteria, and microstructural features are summarized in Table  2 , which provides a foundation for the mechanistic discussions developed throughout this review. Together, these insights frame M/HEAs not merely as new compositions but as a fundamentally different class of superplastic materials whose behavior emerges from the synergy between complex chemistry, metastability, and deformation-driven evolution. Table 2 Comparative assessment of microstructural and mechanistic features of superplasticity in dilute alloys and M/HEAs Characteristic Conventional Alloys (e.g., Al, Ti, Mg) M/HEAs Primary design philosophy Microstructural Stability (Static): Design a fine-grained structure that is resistant to change at forming temperatures. Controlled Microstructural Evolution (Dynamic): Design a metastable structure that evolves into an optimal multi-phase microstructure during deformation. Role of secondary phases Pre-existing, thermally stable particles provide static Zener pinning to inhibit grain growth (e.g., Al 3 Zr, β-phase). Dynamically formed phases (e.g., B2, σ) provide continuous pinning and can participate in strain accommodation. Strain rate sensitivity ( m ) Approaching 0.5 for GBS-dominated flow, indicating diffusion-controlled accommodation. Typically, 0.3–0.4, even for elongations >1000%, suggesting different or cooperative accommodation mechanisms. Dominant accommodation process Diffusion-controlled (grain boundary or lattice diffusion) or conventional dislocation slip. GBS accommodation via a composition- and microstructure-dependent combination of diffusion, dislocation activity, dynamic recrystallization, and phase/interphase-mediated stress relaxation. Chemical complexity may modify these processes through solute drag, short-range order, boundary segregation, and precipitation, but a universally unique dislocation mechanism is yet to be established. Key processing enabler Thermomechanical processing for a stable, recrystallized fine-grain structure. Severe plastic deformation to create a nanocrystalline, highly metastable initial microstructure. Primary microstructural challenge Preventing static grain growth over long forming times at high temperatures. Balancing the formation of beneficial (pinning/accommodating) and detrimental (cavity-nucleating) dynamic phases.

sections.heading: Outlook
paragraphs: Superplasticity in M/HEAs is an emerging field that links fundamental materials science and metallurgy with advanced manufacturing needs. Although these alloys offer exceptional potential for superplastic forming, owing to their thermal stability, fine-grain retention, and tunable boundary chemistry, achieving consistently high elongations across different compositions and processing routes remains challenging. At the same time, the inherent chemical complexity of multicomponent systems creates opportunities that extend beyond the capabilities of classical superplastic alloys. While impressive elongations have been demonstrated under controlled laboratory conditions, broader industrial adoption will depend on clear advantages in forming efficiency, component performance, or lifecycle cost. One possible avenue for reducing cost and enabling large-scale production will be the use of scrap-derived feedstock for alloy casting 121 . As industrial scrap streams continue to expand, incorporating these materials into M/HEA production offers a route toward both environmental sustainability and high-performance alloy design 122 . The resulting improvements in durability and property retention further support the integration of M/HEAs into demanding applications across the aviation, automotive, and energy sectors.

A key limitation is that most exceptional superplastic elongations reported for M/HEAs have been obtained from HPT-processed materials tested using miniature tensile specimens. Owing to radial gradients in strain, grain size, phase constitution, and defect density, the measured elongation is sensitive to specimen geometry, extraction location, and testing methodology. In addition, the high surface-to-volume ratio of miniature specimens can influence cavitation, oxidation, and strain localization. Consequently, these elongations should be viewed as indicators of intrinsic superplastic potential rather than engineering-scale formability. Bridging this gap to industrial application remains a major challenge. Although HPT is unsuitable as a manufacturing route for large components, it provides a powerful platform for identifying the microstructural design principles that enable HSRS, including ultrafine grain size, favorable grain-boundary character, high defect density, and metastable phase stability. Future efforts should focus on reproducing these microstructures through scalable processing routes, such as high-reduction rolling, accumulative roll bonding, ECAP, FSP, powder metallurgy, additive-manufacturing-assisted thermomechanical processing, and continuous severe plastic deformation.

In terms of practical applications, the conflict between promise and difficulty reflects a deeper shift in M/HEA design. Conventional superplastic alloys depend heavily on creating and maintaining microstructural stability: the central task is to produce a fine-grained structure and to suppress coarsening throughout high-temperature deformation. In contrast, recent studies in M/HEAs suggest that microstructural evolution itself (often through controlled metastability) may be harnessed as a productive feature rather than an obstacle. What was once assumed to be thermally stable single-phase alloys is now understood as quasi-single-phase matrices capable of generating secondary or even tertiary phases during deformation 67 , 68 . These emergent phases may assist GBS by offering additional accommodation pathways or by locally restricting grain coarsening, thereby sustaining fine-grained flow. Yet they can also act as hard, non-deforming particles that contribute to cavitation 97 , 98 , introducing a delicate balance between beneficial and detrimental microstructural transformations. Hence, more detailed investigations into the dominant accommodation processes during superplastic deformation of M/HEAs are required.

Following this, modeling emerges as a central tool, not simply as a complement to experiment, but as a necessary framework for navigating the inherent complexity of multicomponent systems 123 . Classical modeling approaches, though powerful, are often insufficient when confronted with the strong chemical disorder, rugged energy landscapes, nonuniform diffusion pathways, and metastable phase transformations that characterize M/HEAs 118 , 119 . Progress will increasingly depend on the integration of multiple modeling paradigms: CALPHAD-based and Machine learning (ML) thermodynamic predictions to map phase equilibria and metastability could help accelerate the discovery of next-generation superplastic M/HEAs; atomistic simulations to examine diffusion, solute clustering, and defect mobility; phase-field models to capture grain growth, coarsening, and transformation pathways; and crystal-plasticity formulations capable of representing GBS, dislocation accommodation, and stress heterogeneity at the mesoscale 124 , 125 .

The convergence of these models with high-resolution, in-situ experimental techniques such as synchrotron diffraction, 4D-STEM, and in-situ TEM promises to bring unprecedented clarity to the dynamic processes occurring during superplastic flow. Particularly important will be the development of constitutive frameworks that link measurable quantities such as strain-rate sensitivity, grain growth kinetics, and cavitation behavior to underlying microstructural mechanisms 126 . Ultimately, the greatest impact of modeling will lie in its ability to bridge length scales: from atomic energetics to mesoscale phase evolution to macroscopic deformation. Through such multi-scale integration, it should become possible to identify chemistries and processing routes that promote dynamically self-stabilizing microstructures, optimize  m , and control phase evolution during high-temperature deformation.

Viewed in a broader perspective, the development of superplastic M/HEAs is not merely an extension of classical alloy design but a reimagining of how superplasticity can be engineered. The challenge moving forward will be to transform these mechanistic insights into predictive frameworks that guide alloy development and industrial implementation. If successful, this new paradigm, rooted in compositional complexity, controlled metastability, and integrated modeling, may redefine the limits of superplastic forming in next-generation materials.

Looking ahead, progress in superplasticity of M/HEAs will rely on exploiting their chemical complexity to engineer alloys with superior formability, stability, and mechanical strength. Advances in scalable processing, grain-boundary engineering, cavitation control, and HSRS activation could enable these alloys to exceed the capabilities of conventional superplastic materials and support next-generation components across aerospace, energy, biomedical, and defense industries.
